Propose, then judge.
A small judge that knows when to ask.

laya-slotjudge-m46 fills the slots of a task-oriented dialogue — city, date, dish, contact… — by choosing among values proposed by cheap extractors, or by answering not specified. Its probability is calibrated, so your assistant can act, ignore or ask the user. With about 0.3 B parameters, it is more accurate than LLM judges of 27 to 180 B parameters.

🤗 Model on Hugging Face Code on GitHub Paper HAL preprint

Why a judge, and why a small one

Large language models are often used to arbitrate between options. They choose well when the right value is there — but they rarely say “nothing was said”. In a dialogue, most slots of a schema are not mentioned in a given turn, and every wrong fill becomes a wrong action.

0.4–0.5 %
of never-mentioned slots wrongly filled, against 15–21 % for the LLMs (MultiATIS++)
3–40×
lower area under the risk–coverage curve: its confidence tells right from wrong
≈ 8 ms
per request on < 2 GiB of GPU memory, against 25–50 ms on one or two full H200 GPUs

Test-set results of the paper (MultiATIS++, MTOP and Multi3WOZ, English and French; monolingual models, same recipe as laya-slotjudge-m46). LLM judges: Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-4-31B-it, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (27–180 B parameters).

How it works

Generation and decision are separated. Proposers are cheap and generous; the judge is small, fast and honest about its doubts.

Move the sliders in the interactive guide →

Propose

Lexicons, a multilingual NER model, the ontology, earlier turns — or an LLM — suggest candidate values for each slot.

Judge

For every slot, one multiple-choice question: the candidates, plus “not specified”. One forward pass scores all the slots of the turn.

Decide

A temperature calibrates the probability; a threshold set for a target risk turns it into act, ignore or ask.

One question per slot

STATE
last_user_message: “a flight from Lyon to Paris on Thursday”
intent: find_flight
QUESTION — slot “from_city” (departure city)
A  Lyon0.97
B  Paris0.01
C  Thursday0.01
D  not specified0.01

The questions are always written in English; the dialogue can be in any of the 46 languages.

What it is — and is not

  • A decision model built on Laya (mmBERT-base encoder + option-scoring head): it chooses, it does not generate.
  • Always offers “not specified”, and is trained to use it — abstention is part of the task.
  • Calibrated: trained with the log score, a strictly proper scoring rule, then temperature-scaled.
  • Not an extractor: it is only as good as its candidates. Pair it with proposers of good recall.

Augmentation must mimic real confusions

Random option lists help on synthetic tests but hurt on real candidates; adding values of the other slots of the utterance as distractors gives robustness at no cost.

Candidates are the bottleneck

A BIO tagger wins when values are literal spans (MultiATIS++, MTOP); the pipeline wins on dialogue (Multi3WOZ), where many gold values are not in the turn.

The model: laya-slotjudge-m46 v1.0

Test results of laya-slotjudge-m46 v1.0 (seed 14, evaluated once). Slot F1 with oracle lists: MTOP 0.95, Multi3WOZ 0.91, MASSIVE 0.90 (0.82 on five languages never seen in training), SGD 0.85 — on par with the monolingual judges of the paper. With the real proposers of the paper: 0.47–0.54, that is 0.06–0.09 below the monolingual judges. Full tables, calibration and decision thresholds on the model card.

Quick start

Install the Laya runtime, download the weights, ask one question per slot. Keep the instruction templates and the “not specified” option exactly as below (in English), and shuffle the candidates.

# pip install "laya>=0.3,<0.4" huggingface_hub
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
from laya import Router

path = snapshot_download("ChristopheCruz/laya-slotjudge-m46", revision="v1.0")
router = Router(models={"multilingual": path})

state = {"last_user_message": "weck mich morgen um sieben Uhr", "intent": "set_alarm"}
options = ["morgen", "sieben Uhr"]
criteria = {chr(65 + i): v for i, v in enumerate(options)}
criteria[chr(65 + len(options))] = "not specified: the last message gives no value for this slot"

question = {
    "type": "choice",
    "instructions": 'Which value does the user\'s last message give for the slot "time" (time of the alarm)?',
    "criteria": criteria,
}
[result] = router.predict_batch([{"state": state, "questions": {"time": question}, "model": "multilingual"}])
print(result["answers"]["time"]["probabilities"])
# {'A': 0.0042, 'B': 0.9834, 'C': 0.0124}

The LayaJudge class of the code repository builds the questions, shuffles the options, groups all the slots of a turn into one call, and implements calibration and the three-zone decision.

Where it fits

Any frequent, well-defined decision among proposed options, where a wrong action costs more than a question.

Assistants and service chatbots

Booking, customer service, support, appointment scheduling — in dozens of languages.

Form filling and extraction

Pick the right value among those found in e-mails, tickets or reports, or flag that it is missing.

AI agents

Choose a tool argument and know when to act alone and when to ask for confirmation.

Replacing LLM judges

Arbitrate between options at a fraction of the cost and latency, with honest probabilities.

Checking an LLM extractor

Pass the generated value and its alternatives as candidates; accept, reject or ask.

Frugal, on-premise deployment

Under 2 GiB of GPU memory, shareable with the other components of the system.

Limitations

  • Candidates bound the result. If the right value is not proposed, the best answer is “not specified”.
  • Position bias remains on ambiguous questions: shuffle the options, write explicit slot descriptions, and average over rotations when it matters.
  • Domain shift. On new domains, fit the temperature and the threshold on your own development data.
  • Most languages are covered by short, translated assistant commands; low-resource languages have fewer examples.
